title: Bringing a Citroën 2CV4 home on a flatbed: the checks to make before the return trip
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: Taking a non-running 2CV4 home is not limited to a matter of booking a trailer. Loading, securing and the first checks on arrival keep a sensible purchase from turning into a fresh problem.
content:
Once the deal had been agreed in the Doubs, the next question was completely practical: the non-running 2CV4, already suffering from very tired floors, had to be loaded and brought back without making its condition worse. Because a 2CV is light, the operation can look simple. In reality, flatbed transport begins with a careful appraisal of the car before the winch even moves.

Prepare the loading before the first metre

Before pulling the car, you need to know whether it still rolls freely, whether the tyres hold enough air and whether the wheels stay reasonably straight. A 2CV that has sat for a long time may have a seized brake, a blocked wheel or a loose panel hanging below the shell. That five-minute check avoids dragging the car crookedly and adding damage to the original problem.

Anything that can move must also be closed or strapped: bonnet, doors, seats, loose parts and the small items collected around the car. In a case like ours, where the main value lay in the completeness of the base, losing a part during loading would have destroyed one of the strongest reasons to buy the car.

Winch line, angle and support points

Winching a tired 2CV has to stay progressive. If the loading angle is too sharp or the hook works poorly, the car puts needless stress on an underside that is already weakened. On an old shell, it is better to lose two minutes realigning the flatbed than to tear a thin section of metal or make the car twist across the ramps.

Support points matter as much as the pull itself. A badly guided wheel or a strap resting on a weak edge can damage in seconds what you intended to save. The correct method is to watch the stance of the car, the wheels and the underside at the same time, not just the speed of the winch.

Secure it for the road, not for a departure photo

Once on the flatbed, the car has to be restrained for a real journey, with vibration, braking and weight transfer. A quick strap placed only to look acceptable in a photo is not enough. On a 2CV, securing has to respect a light shell, thin body panels and an underside that has already been weakened by age.

The sensible reflex is to make one full check again: strap tension, wheel position, loose parts stored away, paperwork collected and one last look underneath. It sounds basic, yet that final check is often the one that prevents a fresh surprise when the car reaches the workshop.

Check everything again once back at the workshop

On arrival, the job does not stop when the car comes off the flatbed. What moved during transport has to be checked, the photographs need to be reviewed and the parts that came back with the car must be listed. On our 2CV4, arriving in Rioz opened the real interpretation of the project: underside, cabin, balance across the whole and the first inventory before dismantling.

The discovery of the car before loading remains on the 2CV4 parent page. The related draft on buying a non-running base completes this logistical step.

Prepare the car before the transporter arrives

The wheels should turn or the carrier must know which are seized and provide a suitable winch. Steering is checked, tyres are inflated only if they can hold pressure and loose objects are removed from the cabin. Hood, doors and bonnet need mechanical closure; adhesive tape alone will not survive wind and vibration. Leaks are declared and absorbent material protects the bed without concealing an active discharge.

Secure through sound structure, never fragile sheet metal

Actual towing combination weight, licences and capacities on the registration documents are checked before departure. Wheel straps hold the car without loading a wing, bumper or pipe. Their angle allows suspension movement without lateral travel. After a few miles, a safe stop permits tension to be checked and confirms that hood, openings and stored parts have not shifted.

Unloading takes place on level ground with a clear path to storage. A car without brakes must never depend on a person standing in front of it. Chocks, winch and assistance control the movement. Photographs before loading and after delivery also record condition for seller, buyer and carrier.
